questions.q: Sound is created when a vibrating object causes particles in a medium to be alternately pushed closer together and spread further apart. What are these two regions called, and what type of wave is sound?
options: Crests and troughs; sound is a transverse wave
Compression (particles closer together) and rarefaction (particles spread apart); sound is a longitudinal wave
Nodes and antinodes; sound is a standing wave
Compression and rarefaction; sound is a transverse wave
questions.explanation: A vibrating object transfers kinetic energy to the medium, producing zones of high air pressure (compression) where particles are pushed closer together and zones of low air pressure (rarefaction) where they are spread apart. These pressure variations travel outwards as a longitudinal wave, in which the air particles oscillate back and forth parallel to the direction of travel.

questions.q: When a sound wave is displayed as a transverse pressure graph, the crest of the transverse wave occurs at the centre of a compression where the pressure is at a maximum. Where does the trough of the transverse wave occur?
options: At the centre of a rarefaction, where the pressure is at a minimum
At the centre of a compression, where the pressure is at a maximum
At a displacement node, where the pressure is normal
At the open end of the pipe, where the pressure is zero
questions.explanation: On a transverse amplitude graph of a sound wave, compressions (higher than normal pressure) are drawn as peaks and rarefactions (lower than normal pressure) as troughs. So the trough occurs at the centre of a rarefaction, where the medium pressure is at a minimum, a quarter-cycle out of step with the displacement.

questions.q: From memory: define the intensity of a sound wave, and explain why the intensity experienced decreases the further you are from a point sound source.
keyPoints: Intensity (I) is the amount of energy a sound wave transfers to a square metre of surface in one second, measured in W m⁻².
Sound waves travel outwards from the source in three dimensions, spreading the acoustic power over the surface of a sphere of ever-increasing radius.
Because that surface area grows with the square of the distance, the intensity is given by I = P / (4πd²), so it falls off as the inverse square of the distance.
questions.explanation: If you recalled that intensity is power delivered per square metre and tied the drop-off to the power being spread over an expanding sphere (area ∝ d²), grade yourself Good or Easy. The intensity at 2 m is one-quarter of that at 1 m, and at 3 m it is one-ninth.

questions.q: The sound intensity 3.0 m from a sound source is 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ W m⁻². Treating the source as a point source, what is the intensity at 1.5 m from the source?
working: Inverse square law for a point source: \(\dfrac{I_2}{I_1} = \dfrac{r_1^{2}}{r_2^{2}}\)
questions.explanation: Since the power of the source is constant, P = 4πr₁²I₁ = 4πr₂²I₂, giving I₂/I₁ = r₁²/r₂². Halving the distance from 3.0 m to 1.5 m quarters the radius-squared denominator, so the intensity rises by a factor of four to 1.6 × 10⁻⁵ W m⁻².

questions.q: From memory, describe the Doppler effect: what is it, what causes it, and what happens to the pitch of a car horn as the car approaches, comes level with you, and then moves away?
keyPoints: The Doppler effect is the apparent shift in the frequency of a sound source heard by an observer.
It results from the movement of the wave source and/or the observer relative to the wave medium.
The pitch of the horn seems higher as the car approaches, then drops as the car comes level with you and moves away — even though the source emits a constant frequency.
questions.explanation: Doppler, who first described the effect in 1842, attributed the apparent frequency shift to relative motion compressing the wavefronts ahead of an approaching source (higher pitch) and stretching them behind a receding source (lower pitch). The emitted frequency never changes; only the observed frequency does.

questions.q: Using the Doppler effect, how does the effective frequency heard by a stationary observer compare with the emitted frequency as a sound source approaches, and then as it moves away?
options: Lower on approach, higher as it moves away
Higher on approach (compressions bunched, shorter effective wavelength), lower as it moves away (compressions spread, longer effective wavelength)
Unchanged on approach, higher as it moves away
Higher both on approach and as it moves away
questions.explanation: As the source approaches, the distance between successive compressions reaching the observer decreases, shortening the effective wavelength and raising the effective frequency above the emitted value. As the source recedes, the effective wavelength increases and the effective frequency drops. The frequency is always heard higher on approach and lower as the source moves away.

questions.q: When two sources of sound of the same amplitude but slightly different frequency are heard together, there is a rhythmic change to the volume of the sound, used to describe beats. As the tuning of the instruments becomes closer, what happens to the beat frequency, and what is it determined by?
options: It increases; determined by the sum of the frequency of the notes played
It decreases until it disappears; determined by the difference in the frequency of the notes played by the different instruments, f_beat = |f₂ − f₁|
It stays constant; determined by the average of the two frequencies
It increases until it disappears; determined by the product of the frequencies
questions.explanation: The beat frequency is determined by the difference in the frequency of the notes played by the different instruments. For two sounds, one at 100 Hz and the other at 120 Hz, the beat frequency is simply found: f_beat = 120 Hz − 100 Hz = 20 Hz, so every 0.05 s a louder beat tone is heard. As the tuning of the instruments becomes closer, the beat frequency decreases until it disappears.

questions.q: Two tuning forks with frequencies of 256 Hz and 262 Hz are placed next to each other and struck so that they vibrate. What beat frequency will be heard?
working: Beat frequency is the magnitude of the difference: \(f_{beat} = |f_2 - f_1|\)
questions.explanation: The beat frequency is simply the size of the difference between the frequencies of the two tuning forks, so |262 − 256| = 6 Hz. The combined sound rises and falls in loudness six times each second.

questions.q: In a pipe closed at one end there is a displacement node at the closed end and a displacement antinode at the open end. Which harmonics does such a closed pipe sustain?
options: All harmonics, whole-number multiples of the fundamental
Only the odd-numbered harmonics (1st, 3rd, 5th … multiples of the fundamental)
Only the even-numbered harmonics (2nd, 4th, 6th …)
Only the fundamental, with no harmonics at all
questions.explanation: The node-at-the-closed-end and antinode-at-the-open-end boundary condition only allows resonant frequencies that are odd multiples of the fundamental: fₙ = (2n + 1)f₀. This is why a pipe closed at one end sustains only the odd-numbered harmonics, giving it a distinctly different tone from an open pipe, which produces all harmonics.

questions.q: What is the fundamental frequency for a pipe closed at one end if it is 0.80 m long and the speed of sound in air is 340 m s⁻¹?
working: For the fundamental of a pipe closed at one end the length holds a quarter wavelength, so \(\lambda_0 = 4L\)
questions.explanation: A pipe closed at one end has a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so its fundamental wavelength is four times the pipe length (λ₀ = 4L = 3.2 m). Applying the wave equation f₀ = v / λ₀ gives 340 / 3.2 = 106.25 Hz ≈ 1.1 × 10² Hz.
